therapy-counselling.summary: Working with a trained professional on self-esteem and body image, so you carry yourself with more confidence alongside any appearance work.

quick.overview:
Therapy or counselling is structured conversation with a trained professional to change thoughts, behaviour and emotional patterns. People bring it into appearance work to build steadier self-esteem and a healthier body image, which shows up as a more confident, relaxed presence.

The chain runs from working through self-esteem issues, to a healthier view of your body, to carrying yourself with more assurance. Psychotherapy has an extensive research base across many conditions; a 2022 umbrella review found generally small effect sizes overall, with different methods often producing similar outcomes. Studies aimed at appearance-specific self-esteem in the looksmaxxing context were not found.
quick.how: People usually see a therapist or counsellor on a regular schedule, often weekly, over weeks to months. Approaches include cognitive-behavioural, humanistic, psychodynamic, systemic and expressive therapies, and many practitioners blend them. Some people use it alongside appearance changes, others in place of them. Many researchers attribute part of the benefit to common factors such as the relationship with the therapist.
quick.risks: Reported limitations include high dropout (roughly 30 to 60 percent), unclear mechanisms of change and uneven outcomes between individuals. Cost and access vary by country. Fit with the therapist matters, and it can take more than one try to find the right one.

angle.text: People use therapy to work through self-esteem and body-image issues, which makes it easier to present yourself with confidence. It is mainstream psychological care with a broad research base, though trials on appearance-specific outcomes are scarce.

journaling-gratitude.summary: Regular reflective writing and gratitude lists that support steadier mood and self-image, so you present yourself with more confidence.

quick.overview:
Journaling is regularly writing down thoughts or experiences; a gratitude journal lists things you are thankful for. People keep one during self-improvement to hold onto a steadier mood and a kinder self-view, which carries into how they present themselves.

The chain is reflective writing, then steadier mood and self-view, then more confident self-presentation. Research summarised on Wikipedia reports short-term mood gains, with longer-lasting effects for daily journals; writing three grateful items daily had some of the longest-lasting effects, strongest around six months. Benefits were greatest in people already inclined to gratitude. The studies measure well-being, not appearance.
quick.how: People write for a few minutes a day, often in the morning or evening, listing a few things they appreciate or noting how the day went. Some pair it with a progress log for gym, skincare or grooming routines so changes are easy to see over time.
quick.risks: No notable physical risks are reported. Studies measured effects over short periods, and the benefit was strongest in people already high in gratitude.

angle.text: Gratitude lists and journals are a reflective habit that steadies mood and self-image during self-improvement, which feeds into a more confident presentation. Small studies show modest well-being effects.

stoicism.summary: An ancient philosophy of focusing on what you control, used to build discipline and ease distress over looks you cannot change.

quick.overview:
Stoicism is a philosophy founded in Athens around 300 BCE by Zeno of Citium. It teaches that virtue is the highest good and that distress comes from false judgments. In self-improvement circles it is used as a framework for discipline and for letting go of worry about parts of your appearance you cannot change.

The chain is focusing on what is controllable, less distress over appearance, then steadier discipline and presence. Wikipedia notes the idea influenced rational emotive behaviour therapy and cognitive behavioural therapy. It is an established philosophy rather than a treatment, and no studies test it for appearance.
quick.how: Practitioners read Stoic writers such as Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius and apply the core exercise of sorting things into what is within their control and what is not. They put effort into habits like training, sleep and grooming and reframe judgments about the rest. Some keep a daily reflection or journal.
quick.risks: No physical risks. It is a philosophy, not a clinical treatment, and it does not replace professional care for anxiety or depression.

angle.text: Self-improvement communities use Stoic ideas to keep effort on controllable habits and to accept what cannot be changed in their looks, which supports discipline and a calmer presence. It is an established philosophy; no studies test it for appearance.

social-media-detox.summary: A deliberate break from social platforms to cut appearance comparison and improve how you see your face and body.

quick.overview:
A social media detox is a set period of reduced or stopped use of platforms. People take one to see fewer idealised faces and bodies, so there is less appearance comparison and a better self-image.

Experiments link viewing idealised images on social networks with higher body dissatisfaction, which is the reasoning behind the break. Meta-analyses of randomised trials report small and sometimes inconsistent effects on well-being; a 2024 meta-analysis found reduced depression but no significant effect on well-being, life satisfaction or stress, and a 2025 study in Body Image compared detox strategies for body image and well-being.
quick.how: People limit or abstain from apps for days to weeks, sometimes using blocking tools or app timers, or delete apps from their phone. Researchers measure well-being, depression, body image and problematic use before and after. Some people return with a trimmed, more selective feed.
quick.risks: No physical risks. Some people report increased fear of missing out or social pressure during a detox, and results across studies are mixed.

angle.text: A break from social platforms cuts exposure to idealised faces and bodies, which means less appearance comparison and a better self-image. Trials show small, mixed effects on well-being, and appearance outcomes are not directly studied.

unfollowing-comparison-accounts.summary: Pruning your feed of accounts that trigger appearance comparison, so you see fewer idealised images and feel better about your own face and body.

quick.overview:
This means unfollowing or muting accounts that make you compare your looks unfavourably. The payoff people want is a calmer self-image and less body dissatisfaction day to day.

The chain is removing comparison-triggering accounts, less exposure to idealised images, then a better body and face image. A systematic review of 43 experimental studies, summarised on Wikipedia, links viewing idealised images on social networking sites with higher body dissatisfaction in young adults, with appearance comparison identified as an important factor. Unfollowing itself has not been tested as an intervention.
quick.how: People go through their following list and unfollow or mute accounts that leave them feeling worse about their appearance, and sometimes follow accounts on other topics instead. Some do this alongside a time limit on apps or a short break.
quick.risks: No physical risks. Long-term effects of content exposure remain unclear, and findings on body-positive content are mixed.

angle.text: People prune their feeds of accounts that provoke appearance comparison to get a healthier view of their own face and body. Experiments link idealised imagery to body dissatisfaction; unfollowing itself has not been studied.

gym-for-confidence-gymmaxxing.summary: Gym training for a leaner, more muscular build and the confidence that tends to come with it; exercise has mood research behind it.

quick.overview:
Gymmaxxing is gym training pursued to improve physique and, as proponents describe it, confidence. The payoff is more muscle, a leaner build and a stronger sense of mastery over your body.

The chain is regular resistance training, then more muscle and a leaner build, then better body satisfaction and confidence. Training effects on muscle are well established. Wikipedia reports that exercise has short- and long-term mood effects and may affect self-esteem, with the strongest evidence for depression, where a 2024 network meta-analysis of 218 trials found exercise comparable to psychotherapy and medication with limited confidence. No study specifically examines gym training as a confidence strategy in looksmaxxing.
quick.how: People follow a regular lifting programme several days a week, usually with progressive overload, and pair it with eating for muscle gain or fat loss. Physique changes typically take months to become visible, and many track photos and lifts to see progress.
quick.risks: Injury risk exists with any training. Evidence on well-being outcomes is mixed, and some people develop an unhealthy fixation on size or leanness.

angle.text: Gym training builds muscle and leanness, and proponents say that visible progress brings more confidence and body satisfaction. Muscle gain is well established, exercise has mood research behind it, and confidence claims have had less direct testing.

cold-exposure-for-mood.summary: Cold showers and plunges used as a discipline habit and mood lift that supports consistent training and routines; carries real cold-shock risks.

quick.overview:
Cold exposure means deliberately taking cold showers or plunging into cold water to feel more alert, resilient and disciplined. In looksmaxxing circles it is grouped with habits that build willpower and energy, so routines like training and grooming stay consistent.

Proponents attribute the effects to the body's stress response to cold and to the act of voluntarily doing something uncomfortable. Cold-water immersion is best studied for athletic recovery: a Cochrane review found some evidence it reduces delayed-onset muscle soreness and perceived fatigue. A 2024 meta-analysis reported an apparent decline in perceived stress within 12 hours, along with improved sleep and quality-of-life scores, in studies of fair to poor quality. None address appearance.
quick.how: People end a normal shower with cold water or use a cold plunge or ice bath for a short time, often in the morning or after training. Some pair it with breathing routines such as the Wim Hof Method. It is used daily or several times a week as a habit.
quick.risks: Medical bodies note risks of hypothermia, circulatory shock and sudden cardiac events from cold-water immersion, and the American Heart Association and British Heart Foundation advise consulting a physician first. Breathing exercises combined with water immersion have been linked in reports to blackout and drowning deaths.

angle.text: Cold showers and plunges are used in looksmaxxing circles as a mood booster and discipline habit that keeps routines like training consistent. Small studies report lower perceived stress and better sleep; none address appearance.

dopamine-detox.summary: A temporary break from phones, porn and junk food to regain motivation for gym, grooming and study routines; the neurochemical reset idea is disputed by neuroscientists.

quick.overview:
A dopamine detox means pulling back from stimulating habits such as social media, gaming, junk food and pornography for a set period. In ascension circles it is used to regain focus and motivation so gym, grooming and study routines get done, sometimes alongside no-masturbation challenges.

It was popularised in 2019 by psychologist Cameron Sepah as a behavioural tool for compulsive habits, and he has said the name is misleading since the aim is to reduce impulsive behaviour, not lower dopamine. Neuroscientists say dopamine drives motivation and learning and cannot be reset by avoiding stimuli. No large trials test it directly; related reviews of social-media detoxes report a small reduction in depressive symptoms.
quick.how: People set a period, from a day to a few weeks, in which they cut phones, social media, gaming, junk food or porn, and fill the time with exercise, reading or study. Some forum users report feeling focused afterward, while others report feeling flat.
quick.risks: Extreme versions may worsen anxiety, loneliness or restrictive habits, and the practice is not a treatment for addiction or depression. Some people describe withdrawal-like symptoms when quitting substances alongside it.

angle.text: Ascension circles use temporary abstinence from stimulating activities to regain motivation for gym, grooming and study routines. The idea that it resets brain chemistry is disputed by neuroscientists, and no appearance outcomes have been tested.

self-improvement-glow-up-content.summary: Before-and-after transformation videos and posts that show the methods behind a changed look, used as templates and motivation.

quick.overview:
Glow-up content is the genre of before-and-after videos and posts showing someone's changed appearance, often crediting skincare, fitness, grooming, clothing or procedures. Viewers use them as examples of what is possible and as templates for their own changes.

The chain is seeing the before-and-after, learning the methods credited, then copying changes to your own looks. It is a social-media descendant of the makeover genre, which has long featured in daytime talk shows, personal makeover television series and film. Few published sources study social-media transformation content specifically.
quick.how: People watch or save transformation posts, note the haircut, skincare routine, clothing or training approach credited, and try them. Many also post their own progress photos to track and share changes over time.
quick.risks: Before-and-after posts are selected and edited, so lighting, angles and timing can account for part of the difference. Related research links social-media exposure to appearance comparison, so some people find the genre motivating and others find it discouraging.

angle.text: Transformation videos and posts show before-and-after changes in clothing, haircuts, skin, fitness or procedures, and viewers use them as templates and motivation for their own changes. The genre is popular; few studies examine it.

glow-up.summary: Slang for a marked improvement in appearance, from grooming and skincare to cosmetic procedures; the core goal of looksmax forum culture.

quick.overview:
A glow up is a noticeable improvement in how someone looks, usually over weeks to years. The term covers everything from skincare and haircuts to fillers and rhinoplasty, and it appears across looksmax forums in thread titles such as '30 day glow up' guides and personal transformation stories.

The chain is grooming, skincare and fitness changes, then cumulative visible improvement, then a marked before-and-after difference. It is documented mostly through testimonials and photos. Published research on the term is minimal; a 2024 Frontiers in Psychiatry study named a professional photoshoot intervention for adolescent psychiatric patients 'Glow up'.
quick.how: Posters describe combining skincare, hydration, diet, exercise, haircuts and facial hair grooming, and sometimes cosmetic procedures. A common starting point is a generic 30-day plan covering the basics, with larger changes added over time. Some users note that better skin, lighting or photo angles also contribute to how a transformation looks.
quick.risks: Risks depend on the method, from none for basic grooming to those of filler and surgery. Some testimonials describe bullying, insecurity or an eating disorder as the background to a transformation.

angle.text: A glow up is a marked improvement in appearance built from small grooming, skincare and fitness changes that add up, and in some cases cosmetic procedures. It is documented mostly through testimonials and before-and-after photos.

social-skills-game-pickup.summary: Pickup 'game' trains confidence and conversation alongside fitness, style and grooming to improve attraction; the community draws strong criticism.

quick.overview:
'Game' is the pickup community's term for skills in meeting and attracting partners, split into inner game (confidence, psychology) and outer game (social skills, fitness, fashion, grooming). In looksmaxxing it is often discussed as a complement to appearance, to turn good looks into actual attraction.

The chain is practising social skills and confidence, building the outer game of fitness, style and grooming, and arriving at stronger presence. It spread through online forums from the 1990s and reached the mainstream with Neil Strauss's 2005 book The Game. Some commentators say there is no evidence its claims work, while others say principles such as generating attraction and building rapport have some support in social and evolutionary psychology.
quick.how: Practitioners approach people repeatedly, practise conversation, and follow staged sequences from attraction to comfort. Many buy workshops, books or coaching, and combine it with gym, style and grooming work. Some schools use NLP-derived methods, which scientific consensus treats as pseudoscience.
quick.risks: Critics describe parts of the movement as sexist or misogynistic, and the Southern Poverty Law Center characterises it as male supremacist. Specific tactics such as 'negging' and last-minute-resistance techniques have drawn criticism, and some instructors have faced travel bans after videos of unwanted physical contact.

angle.text: Pickup communities teach inner game (confidence) and outer game (fitness, fashion, grooming) so looks translate into attraction. Some principles have academic support, the community draws strong criticism, and effectiveness claims have not been tested.

charisma-training.summary: Practising the posture, gestures and vocal delivery associated with charisma to come across as more compelling; research suggests some of these behaviours can be taught.

quick.overview:
Charisma training means practising the behaviours people associate with presence, such as posture, gestures and vocal delivery. In appearance-focused circles it is treated as a complement to physical looks, so you come across as more magnetic and engaging.

Perceived charisma depends partly on the speaker's nonverbal and vocal behaviour and partly on how others perceive it, following Max Weber's relational view. Wikipedia reports that studies of recorded speakers and experiments show posture, gestures and prosody influence perceived charisma, and that some of these behaviours can be taught, citing a 2011 paper by Antonakis, Fenley and Liechti, 'Can Charisma be Taught? Tests of Two Interventions'. Few sources connect it to looksmaxxing specifically.
quick.how: People rehearse open posture, deliberate gestures and varied vocal tone, often by recording themselves or practising speeches and conversations. Some read books such as Olivia Fox Cabane's The Charisma Myth or take speaking courses. Changes build with repeated practice over weeks.
quick.risks: No specific risks are documented. The concept of charisma remains ambiguous among scholars, and results depend on audience and context.

angle.text: Users practise the posture, gesture and vocal behaviours associated with charisma to come across as more compelling and present. Research suggests some of these behaviours can be taught.

exposure-therapy-for-social-anxiety.summary: Gradually facing feared social situations to lower anxiety, so you interact with more ease; a core CBT technique with a sizeable trial literature.

quick.overview:
Exposure therapy has a person face feared social situations step by step, so that anxiety fades with experience. People use it so the work they put into their appearance turns into relaxed, confident interaction rather than avoidance.

The chain is gradually facing feared situations, less social anxiety, then a more relaxed presence. It is a central part of CBT, the first-line psychotherapy for social anxiety disorder, and research covers real-life, imagined and virtual reality exposure. The trial evidence concerns diagnosed social anxiety, not appearance goals. Repeated contact with the feared situation without real danger is thought to produce new safety learning, though mechanism research is still developing.
quick.how: Exposure is organised as a hierarchy that moves from less to more feared situations, such as speaking up in a group, then starting conversations or speaking in public. It is usually delivered by a clinician in CBT, and some people adapt it as self-directed practice. Gains typically build over a series of sessions.
quick.risks: Anxiety typically rises temporarily during exposure. Evidence relates to diagnosed social anxiety, and clinicians usually deliver the treatment, so people with significant anxiety are generally directed to professional care.

angle.text: People use graded exposure to reduce social anxiety so their appearance work translates into confident interaction. It is a core CBT technique for social anxiety disorder with a sizeable trial literature, though appearance outcomes are not its target.

approach-anxiety-challenges.summary: Daily self-set tasks of starting conversations with strangers to dull social nerves and build a more confident presence.

quick.overview:
Approach anxiety challenges are small daily tasks in which someone starts interactions with strangers to get used to the nervousness. They are used in dating and social-confidence communities, including some looksmaxxing spaces, to build social confidence alongside appearance work.

The chain is daily approaches to strangers, less social nervousness, then a more confident presence. The practice has not been studied by name, but its structure resembles graded exposure, the technique used in CBT for social anxiety disorder, where facing feared situations repeatedly is thought to reduce fear and avoidance.
quick.how: People set a daily or weekly target, such as saying hello to a set number of strangers, asking for directions or starting a short chat, and make the tasks gradually harder. Some keep a tally or log in a journal or with a group. Many report the nerves easing over weeks of repetition.
quick.risks: No documented harms specific to the practice. Clinical sources direct people with severe social anxiety toward professional treatment such as CBT, and it helps to respect others' signals when approaching strangers.

angle.text: Dating-advice and some looksmaxxing communities use daily challenges of starting conversations with strangers to build social confidence alongside appearance work. The practice has not been studied directly, though it resembles the graded exposure used in CBT.

eye-contact-practice.summary: Training steady gaze in conversation so you come across as more engaged, confident and present.

quick.overview:
Eye contact practice means training yourself to hold someone's gaze during conversation so you seem more present, assured and engaged. Eye contact is a well-described form of nonverbal communication, studied as oculesics.

The chain is training a steady gaze, seeming more engaged and assured, then leaving a more confident impression. Wikipedia reports that eye contact can signal interest, forms part of flirting, and is linked in some contexts to confidence and respect, while norms differ widely between cultures. Published research on structured eye contact training is limited.
quick.how: People rehearse holding gaze in everyday conversation, often starting with shorter holds and breaking away naturally, or practising with a friend or mirror. It is typically built up over weeks of ordinary interactions.
quick.risks: Prolonged unbroken eye contact can feel overbearing, and people with autism or social anxiety may find it distressing. Cultural norms differ on how much is appropriate.

angle.text: Users practise holding eye contact so they appear more confident, engaged and present in conversation. Eye contact is well described as nonverbal communication, and norms vary across cultures.

self-compassion-practice.summary: Treating yourself kindly after setbacks instead of harsh self-criticism, for a healthier body image during appearance work.

quick.overview:
Self-compassion practice means responding to your own perceived flaws or failures with kindness, a sense of shared humanity and mindful awareness, following Kristin Neff's model. In body-image contexts it is used as an alternative to harsh self-criticism during appearance work, so setbacks do not turn into spirals.

The chain is treating yourself kindly after setbacks, less harsh self-criticism, then a healthier body image. Wikipedia reports that self-compassion is associated with lower depression, anxiety, rumination, perfectionism and disordered eating attitudes, mainly in correlational and well-being research. Appearance-specific trials are lacking.
quick.how: Practices include self-kind phrasing, recognising that others struggle too, and observing painful feelings without over-identifying with them. Formal programmes such as Mindful Self-Compassion exist, and some people use short daily exercises or journaling.
quick.risks: No documented harms in the sources reviewed. One 2025 study suggests rumination may hinder the effects after a body image threat.

angle.text: Self-compassion is used during appearance work to replace harsh self-criticism with kindness, supporting a healthier body image. It is linked to better well-being, mainly in correlational research.

body-neutrality-body-positivity.summary: Two body-image stances, valuing all bodies or making looks matter less, used to ease appearance anxiety and relax self-presentation.

quick.overview:
Body positivity promotes a positive view of all bodies; body neutrality holds that appearance should matter as little as possible and sometimes focuses on what the body can do. People adopt them to ease appearance anxiety and feel more relaxed in how they present themselves.

Both aim to loosen appearance-contingent self-worth, through affirmation (positivity) or de-emphasis of looks (neutrality). Early experiments suggest both types of content may improve body image compared with appearance-ideal content, though the studies are short, recent and mostly online. Body positivity has roots in the fat acceptance movement, and body neutrality emerged around 2015 as a middle path.
quick.how: People follow accounts and content that reflect the stance, use affirmations or body-function framing, and cut back on appearance-focused content. Some combine either stance with training or grooming goals.
quick.risks: Critics note body positivity can keep attention on appearance or suppress negative feelings, and some argue it may weaken health motivation. Evidence on long-term effects is limited.

angle.text: Body positivity and body neutrality are stances people adopt to ease appearance anxiety, either by valuing all bodies or by making looks matter less, for a more relaxed self-presentation. Early experiments look at social media content rather than physical change.

intuitive-eating.summary: Eating by hunger and fullness cues instead of diet rules, for a calmer relationship with food and body; linked to better psychological outcomes.

quick.overview:
Intuitive eating, created by dietitians Evelyn Tribole and Elyse Resch, replaces diet rules with attention to hunger, fullness and satisfaction. People use it to cut diet stress and bingeing and to settle into a stable weight and better body satisfaction.

Its ten principles include rejecting the diet mentality, honouring hunger and fullness, making peace with food and coping with emotions without food. Their book Intuitive Eating was first published in 1995. Reviews link it with better psychological outcomes, while evidence on long-term weight and physical health is limited or mixed.
quick.how: People stop counting and restricting, eat when hungry and stop when comfortably full, and allow all foods. It is common in eating disorder recovery and body image circles, often with guidance from a dietitian. It is a change in approach built up over months rather than a short programme.
quick.risks: It is not a weight-loss method, and long-term weight data are limited. Some medical conditions need structured diets, and the lack of concrete rules can make it hard to apply.

angle.text: Intuitive eating swaps diet rules for hunger and fullness cues, aiming for less diet stress and bingeing and a steadier weight and body satisfaction. It has good psychological correlates; evidence on weight change is weaker.

eating-disorder-recovery.summary: The process of recovering from an eating disorder and returning to regular eating, toward a healthier body and body image.

quick.overview:
Eating disorder recovery is the process of getting better from conditions such as anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa and binge eating disorder. It means a return to regular eating and quitting restrictive habits, with physical and psychological recovery and a healthier body and body image.

Researchers say there are almost as many definitions of recovery as studies, with a trend toward including physical, behavioural and psychological components. In looksmaxxing forums, recovery posts appear alongside discussion of leanness and diet, where some members describe returning to regular eating as part of a wider personal reset. Wikipedia reports about 70% of people with anorexia nervosa and 50% with bulimia recover within five years.
quick.how: Treatment varies by disorder and can include counselling, dietary guidance, reducing excessive exercise and food avoidance, medication for associated symptoms, and hospitalisation in serious cases. Research highlights social support, social identity and perfectionism as factors. It is typically delivered by a clinical team.
quick.risks: Both anorexia and bulimia increase the risk of death, and only about 10% of people with eating disorders receive treatment. Anyone affected is generally directed to medical and mental health professionals.

angle.text: Recovery is discussed in looksmaxxing and diet communities as a return to regular eating and leaving restrictive habits behind, for a healthier body and body image. Researchers note there is no single agreed definition, spanning physical, behavioural and psychological change.

muscle-dysmorphia-bigorexia.summary: A body-image condition where muscular people feel too small, recognised in psychiatry and discussed in lifting circles as 'bigorexia'.

quick.overview:
Muscle dysmorphia is a subtype of body dysmorphic disorder in which a person believes their body is too small or not muscular enough, even when already muscular. It is often called bigorexia or reverse anorexia, and in lifting and looksmaxxing circles it comes up around size, leanness and perceived smallness.

Clinicians describe a distorted perception of one's muscularity driving compulsive training, dietary rules and overtraining. Reported risk factors include steroid use, trauma, bullying, perfectionism, low self-esteem and exposure to idealised muscular bodies. Prevalence estimates range from about 1% to 54% of men in different groups, higher among gym members, weightlifters, bodybuilders and steroid users; a study of 384 male bodybuilders found 5.7% reported it.
quick.how: It is a clinical condition rather than a technique. Treatment research is limited, mostly case reports; family-based therapy, cognitive behavioural therapy and SSRIs have some supporting evidence according to Wikipedia's summary. Recognition and referral by clinicians and trainers is part of care.
quick.risks: Reported consequences include co-occurring eating, mood, anxiety and substance use disorders, social avoidance, injury from overtraining and use of performance-enhancing drugs. A 2026 review proposes a link between bigorexia-related behaviours and early cardiovascular injury in adolescents.

angle.text: Lifting and looksmaxxing circles discuss bigorexia as the body-image condition in which muscular people feel insufficiently big, driving compulsive training and eating that reshape the physique. It is recognised in psychiatry as a subtype of body dysmorphic disorder.
